newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish KPW says price-fixing case biggest ever.
newsitem.headline: Polish KPW says price-fixing case biggest ever.

text.p: Suspicions of price manipulation on the Warsaw bourse announced by the Securities Commission (KPW) late on Tuesday represent the largest such case since Poland resumed bourse trade in 1991, the KPW's spokeswoman said.

On Tuesday the KPW notified the public prosecutor that a group of investors may have illegally manipulated prices, which is punishable by up to three years in prison and a fine of up to five million zlotys ($1.4 million).
"I think we can say that the size, considering the number of individuals and the time over which it took place, (represents) the large manipulation," Beata Stelmach told Reuters on Wednesday.
She said the KPW investigated the matter for over a year.
Bourse president Wieslaw Rozlucki defined the crime as a group of investors colluding to buy or sell a particular stock and thereby artificially moving its price.
Officials at the bourse, KPW and prosecutor's office have given no details on the matter.

Weekly magazine Wprost, however, wrote in its issue appearing on Wednesday that a group of 20 investors from the western city of Poznan made more than 50 million zlotys during two years speculating on three firms on the parallel market.
Andrzej Jozwiak, head of the orgainised crime department of the Poznan prosecutor's office, told Reuters that for now there were no suspects in the investigation that was only a week old.
Analysts said main market sentiment would not likely be hurt by the news of alleged price-fixing because the allegations largely involved less-liquid parallel market firms.
"Paradoxically, large-cap firms might be helped as players are cautious about investing in smaller ones," said Roman Sosnowski, an analyst at WBK AIB Asset Management.
Stelmach said Polish securities law sufficiently regulated bourse trade but could not guarantee there would be no breaches of the law.

"The Polish market is safe and transparent....The law is not defective....By a regulation we are not able to ensure that no one will steal," she said, adding that it was necessary simply to catch and punish any law-breaker.

Stelmach also said that currently there were more than a dozen cases of possible illegal practices concerning public trade which had reached the Commission, of which six involve crimes using insider information or price manipulation.
Rozlucki said that each year the bourse informs the KPW of 30 to 40 cases in which prices rise sharply for no apparent reason.
He said the bourse's 10-percent daily price-fluctuation limit helped give investors enough time to analyse price moves.
